recipes.instructions: Write a grammatical declarative sentence with present/past be or have/has, or an explicit habitual action every morning/day/evening/night/week. Vary pronouns, ordinary subjects, and singular heads with plural modifiers, such as the box of cables. Avoid read, questions, collective-noun agreement, subjunctives and ambiguous tense choices.
constraints: Change agreement within the same tense and verb family only
One explicit subject controls the edited verb
Some modifier constructions intentionally exceed present decoder guards
examples: She is ready for the workshop.
The box of cables is beside the desk.
They work at the library every morning.

recipes.instructions: Write a grammatical sentence containing a or an immediately before one of: apple, orange, egg, umbrella, envelope, idea, hour, honest, honor, heir, book, pencil, bicycle, camera, notebook, ticket, friend, message, pen, project, library, university, user, unicorn, european, one. Use pronunciation exceptions naturally and vary the rest of the sentence.
constraints: Unknown acronyms and pronunciation classes are not guessed
examples: We waited for an hour outside the office.
She received a university application yesterday.

recipes.instructions: Write a grammatical possession sentence with has/have followed by a/an and a singular countable object, preferably at sentence end: book, pencil, bicycle, camera, notebook, ticket, message, pen, project, apple, orange, egg, umbrella, envelope, idea. Avoid noun compounds and mass nouns. Vary the subject and context.
constraints: Delete an existing verified indefinite article
Reject noun compounds and modifiers that make noun-head status uncertain
examples: Our new colleague has an umbrella.
They have a ticket for the afternoon train.

recipes.instructions: Write a grammatical sentence with two/three/four/five/six/seven/eight/nine/ten followed by a regular plural head noun: books, pencils, bicycles, cameras, notebooks, tickets, messages, pens, projects, apples, oranges, eggs, umbrellas, envelopes, ideas, libraries. The noun must be a head, not a compound modifier, and should end the sentence or be followed by a prepositional phrase.
constraints: Explicit numeral and closed singular/plural mapping
examples: We bought three tickets for the evening show.
The neighborhood has two libraries.

recipes.instructions: Write a grammatical direct question beginning Do or Does followed immediately by I/you/we/they/he/she/it and a base-form verb. Vary the predicate and objects. Keep modal and indirect questions for clean controls, not this recipe.
constraints: Edit only the initial do/does auxiliary
Preserve the already-correct lexical base form
Explicit question mark and subject pronoun
examples: Does she need another ticket for the trip?
Do they know the meeting location?

recipes.instructions: Write a grammatical perfect construction containing has/have/had immediately followed by eaten/taken/broken/chosen/written/gone/seen. Vary subjects, objects and context. Avoid dialect-dependent participles, adjective readings, and changes to tense or aspect.
examples: They have eaten lunch before the appointment.
Mara had written the instructions before the workshop.

recipes.instructions: Write natural grammatical sentences using much before information/advice/equipment/furniture/homework/traffic, or many before books/tickets/messages/projects/pencils. Negative sentences and questions often make much natural. Avoid ambiguous count/mass nouns such as paper, chicken, experience, work, coffee and time.
constraints: No intervening modifier or noun compound
examples: We do not have much information about the event.
The team received many messages after the announcement.

recipes.instructions: Write a grammatical sentence using one lexical frame: rely/relies/relied on, depend/depends/depended on, interested in, responsible for, or similar to. Follow the preposition with an ordinary explicit object. Avoid quoted text, particles, location readings and dialect-disputed constructions.
constraints: Do not treat stylistic alternatives as errors
examples: We rely on this map during the trip.
She is interested in the new exhibition.
The volunteer is responsible for the equipment.

recipes.instructions: Write a grammatical natural sentence with the, a, an, can, or because in an ordinary nonquoted use. Avoid deliberate emphatic repetition, dialogue hesitation, and metalinguistic examples.
constraints: Never mutate grammatical had had or that that
examples: We can finish the report before lunch.
The meeting starts after the demonstration.

recipes.instructions: Write valid English that must remain unchanged. Include informal lowercase messages, questions with auxiliaries and modals, names, technical vocabulary, simple past read, grammatical had had/that that, subjunctives and mass nouns. Informal initial lowercase is intentional and must be preserved. Vary the wording rather than copying these examples.
constraints: Exact identity including case and whitespace
examples: my dog is sleepy.
Did Mara read the report yesterday?
If she were here, she would help.
The teacher had had a busy week.
We agreed that that answer was correct.
